findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Resolve the claim-vs-transition bare-`--force` divergence in the argparse design: claim (claim.py:44-46) consumes a following space-separated non-flag token as the reason, transition (transition.py:175-177) does not — state per-command whether that space-separated form is preserved or is an intended (documented) behavior change.
evidence: Plan: 'the `--force[=<reason>]` reason-carrying bypass (bare `--force` -> "(no reason given)"; `--force=<reason>` -> that reason)'
claim.py:44-46: bare `--force` returns the NEXT token as the reason when it exists and does not start with `--` (space-separated value consumed)
transition.py:175-177: bare `--force` sets force_reason="" and advances i by 1 — the next token is NOT consumed
findings.finding: The plan treats claim and transition --force as identically spellable under one argparse pattern, but claim's bare --force space-consumes a following non-flag token as the reason while transition's does not — a divergence a single nargs='?' spec cannot reproduce.
scenarios: `rebar claim <id> --force some-reason` today records 'some-reason' as the audit note; an argparse const-only mapping would record '(no reason given)' and mis-parse 'some-reason'
Migrating both commands onto one shared parser spec silently changing claim's bare-force value-capture behavior
findings.suggested_fix: Decide and record explicitly: either preserve claim's space-consume via a custom action/nargs='?' with positional disambiguation, or (if space-form capture is deemed vestigial) call it out as an accepted behavior change with a test — do not leave it implicit under 'preserve exactly'.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Resolve exactly how argparse will realize `--force[=<reason>]` (e.g. nargs='?' + const='(no reason given)') and confirm it preserves each current parser's token-consumption behavior — including that transition's bare `--force` must NOT swallow a following space-separated token as _parse_flags does today.
evidence: Plan: '--force[=<reason>] reason-carrying bypass (bare --force -> "(no reason given)"; --force=<reason> -> that reason) ... must be preserved exactly'
claim.py _parse_force lines 44-46: bare `--force` looks ahead — `nxt if nxt and not nxt.startswith('--') else '(no reason given)'` (space-separated token IS consumed)
transition.py _parse_flags lines 175-176: `elif a == '--force': force_reason = ''` (bare --force does NOT consume the next token)

Prior art (docs.python.org/3/library/argparse, StackOverflow 30896982) confirms nargs='?'+const is the optional-value idiom AND that with nargs='?' a present option string may or may not be followed by a value the parser will greedily bind
findings.finding: The plan asserts argparse 'preserves exactly' the --force[=<reason>] optional-value form and the --assignee None-vs-empty-string distinction, but does not resolve HOW argparse realizes these semantics — the canonical nargs='?'+const idiom greedily consumes a following space-separated token as the value, and the two current parsers differ on precisely that point (claim's _parse_force consumes `--force <next>` as the reason; transition's _parse_flags does not), so a naive migration risks a behavior change.
scenarios: `ticket transition abc1 closed --force somearg` where somearg is a non-flag token — argparse nargs='?' would bind it as the force reason; today _parse_flags leaves force_reason='' and treats somearg as an unknown skipped token
`ticket claim abc1 --force reason` — must still yield reason as the note to match today's _parse_force
findings.suggested_fix: State the concrete argparse construct per flag: `--force` as nargs='?' with const='(no reason given)'; `--assignee` as a plain store with default=None (NOT nargs='?') so absent=>None and explicit ''=>cleared are distinct; and note the nargs='?' space-token greediness, calling out whether transition's bare-`--force` non-consumption is preserved or intentionally normalized.
